scenes.headline: How a plot style becomes a skill
scenes.sub: Eight papers' scripts, data and figures, with the rules written down.
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Plum! A Yale researcher packaged his paper-plotting style as a skill for coding agents. Here's how it's built, and what its own figures show.

scenes.text: Commit each script beside its data and figure, and a house style becomes checkable.
scenes.say: Commit each script beside its data and the figure it made, and a house style becomes checkable, not a matter of taste.

steps.say: An agent reads the skill file first. It's a router: when to use the style, when not to, and which file to open.
Five reference files hold the rules. The design theory file is almost all numbers: font sizes, line widths, resolution, nine hex codes.
The canonical examples are the figure folders. Each keeps its script, its data and the image it produced, side by side.

steps.note: None of the nine functions exist in the repository
steps.say: One file specifies nine helper functions. None exist, so every agent session writes its own, and the consistency slips.

items.say: Drop the top and right spines. They encode nothing.
Paint your own method one dark blue.
Greens for improvements, reds for baselines. Under deuteranopia, that pair nearly merges.
And print the value on every bar.

scenes.title: The rule that is missing
scenes.say: One rule is missing. The headline figure starts its y-axis at zero point five, so a bar's height isn't its score.

parts.say: The two scores differ by one point six four times.
and the drawn bars differ ten times. A bar's length is its encoding.

scenes.text: A style guide for agents needs a checker, not a spec, and a bar's length is its encoding.

scenes.say: To recap: commit the outputs, route the agent, and make the rules a checker.
